title: Two-Photon Bound States in the Continuum: A No-Go Theorem and Long-Lived Quasi-Bound States
abstract: Two-photon bound states in the continuum provide a stringent setting in which quantum interference must suppress radiative decay despite photon--photon interactions. Here, we prove a no-go theorem showing that a single nonlinear mode linearly coupled to a noninteracting bosonic continuum cannot support an interaction-active two-photon bound state in the continuum, provided the local spectral density vanishes only at isolated energies. Apart from this regularity condition, the result is independent of the continuum dispersion and the frequency-dependent coupling. Although such an exact bound state is forbidden, long-lived two-photon quasi-bound states remain possible. For a giant Kerr cavity nonlocally coupled to a waveguide, we derive the asymptotic scaling of the two-photon decay rate with the coupling-point separation from weak nonlinearity to the hard-core limit. We further identify a regime in which the two-photon resonance is substantially longer lived than the single-photon excitation. Our work establishes the limits of exact multiphoton confinement while opening a route to engineering long-lived interacting few-photon states.
summary: This theoretical paper proves a no-go theorem forbidding exact two-photon Bound States in the Continuum when photon-photon interactions are active. Crucially, it shows that while exact states are forbidden, long-lived quasi-bound states can be engineered by coupling nonlinear modes to continua. This opens pathways for controlling few-photon quantum dynamics beyond single-excitation limits.
main_problem: The research investigates the existence of exact two-photon Bound States in the Continuum (BICs) when photon-photon interactions are present, and explores conditions for realizing long-lived quasi-bound states.
main_result: A no-go theorem proves that interaction-active two-photon BICs cannot exist under standard regularity conditions. However, long-lived quasi-bound states can be engineered, potentially achieving lifetimes much longer than single-photon excitations.
method: The analysis relies on solving the BIC condition using Green's functions and pair bubble propagators ($\Pi(z)$), analyzing decay rates ($\kappa^2$) in weak and strong nonlinearity limits.
model_or_system: The model consists of a single nonlinear bosonic mode coupled linearly to a noninteracting bosonic continuum (e.g., a waveguide). Specific examples include giant Kerr cavities coupled to waveguides.
key_observables: Two-photon decay rates ($\kappa_2$), the ratio $\kappa_1/\kappa_2$, and the spectral density properties of the continuum.
important_parameters: Nonlinearity strength ($U$), coupling point separation ($d$), detuning ($\delta_0$), and the nature of the local spectral density.
main_assumptions: The no-go theorem assumes that the local one-photon spectral density vanishes only at isolated energies. Quasi-BIC analysis often focuses on limits like weak nonlinearity or large/small coupling separations.
figures_summary: Figure 1 schematically classifies two-photon BICs based on interaction activity. Figure 2 compares calculated decay rates ($\kappa^2$) for quasi-BICs in small-$d$ and large-$d$ regimes, while Figure 3 shows the scaling of these rates in the hard-core limit.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the Hamiltonian and BIC condition using Green's functions. It first proves the no-go theorem for interaction-active states. Subsequently, it analyzes the possibility of quasi-BICs by examining decay rate scaling ($\kappa^2$) across different coupling regimes (weak vs. strong nonlinearity) to demonstrate lifetime engineering.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant as it pushes the boundaries of controlling light-matter interactions in open quantum systems, demonstrating how nonlinearities can be used to engineer coherence and extend confinement times beyond what simple single-photon analysis predicts.
